definition: Deafening means so overwhelmingly loud that, for the moment, nothing else can be heard.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word deafening. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know deafening should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The jets passed low over the parade route, and for three deafening seconds every conversation along the avenue simply stopped.
Noisy is far milder than deafening: a noisy cafe makes you raise your voice, while a deafening one would erase your voice altogether.
Thunderous goes further than noisy — a deep boom that fills the whole air; deafening claims the most: noise so total that hearing shuts down for everything else.
Ear-splitting is about pain — a shriek or alarm so sharp it feels like a blade in the ear. Deafening is about totality: the sound may not even hurt, but it swallows every other sound whole.
Roaring describes the texture of big noise — the continuous, engulfing rush of a crowd or a waterfall. Deafening states the effect: whatever the texture, nothing else can be heard through it.
so soft it can barely be heard
deliberately quieted, kept low

Deafening never passed through Latin at all. It is plain Old English deaf wearing the verb-making suffix -en — the same -en that turns dark into darken and hard into harden. When you meet a de- word, check what is left after the prefix: if 'afening' means nothing, the de- was never a prefix to begin with.
Deafening means so overwhelmingly loud that, for the moment, nothing else can be heard.
The mill's stamping press ran day and night, and new hires learned its lesson within an hour: on the floor, the noise was deafening.
Foremen gave orders in hand signals; the lunch whistle was a light bulb, not a whistle, because no whistle could climb over the machines.
Workers who wanted to talk stepped into the stairwell and pulled the door shut — and even there, they shouted.
Deafening is the exact word for the press floor because the noise does not merely annoy — it swallows hearing itself, so completely that whistles, warnings, and voices all disappear into it.
Loud describes any strong sound; deafening claims the total kind, the noise that leaves your ears nothing else.
vivid, journalistic — reaches easily into figurative use

Deafening is the loudness ladder's ceiling, and writers borrow it for one famous figure: the deafening silence, a quiet so pointed it drowns out everything the way noise would — the word still means 'nothing else gets through.' Keep it off small annoyances and out of the other senses: a glaring color or an overpowering flavor is loud only by metaphor, and neither can deafen.
And keep it aimed at the noise, not the hearer — a person losing hearing is going deaf, not growing deafening.

For the two seconds of each strike, the world has one sound in it.
Coworkers' mouths move; the radio playing by the lockers stops existing.
Veterans time their conversations to the gaps, trading half-sentences between strikes the way pedestrians cross between waves of traffic.
By the end of a week, new workers do it too, without noticing they have learned.
